problem.summary: 机器学习模型大多是黑盒，用户难以理解预测背后的原因，这影响了对预测和模型的信任，进而影响模型的实际应用和部署。

motivation.summary: 信任是有效使用机器学习系统的关键。用户需要理解预测原因以决定是否采取行动，也需要评估模型整体可靠性。现有方法（如验证集准确率）不足以揭示模型在真实世界数据上的行为或识别数据泄露、数据集偏移等问题。

core_idea.summary: 提出LIME（Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations），通过在预测实例周围学习一个局部可解释模型来解释任何分类器的预测。同时提出SP-LIME（Submodular Pick LIME），通过子模优化选择一组有代表性的实例及其解释，以提供对模型的全局理解。

method.summary: LIME通过扰动输入实例，观察黑盒模型的输出变化，在局部拟合一个可解释的线性模型（如稀疏线性模型）。SP-LIME基于解释矩阵，通过子模优化选择一组实例，以最大化对重要特征的覆盖，同时避免冗余。

experiments.summary: 在文本（情感分析、宗教分类）和图像（狼与哈士奇分类）任务上，使用多种黑盒模型（决策树、逻辑回归、SVM、随机森林、神经网络）进行模拟和真人实验。评估解释的忠实度、对个体预测的信任评估、模型选择能力以及帮助改进不可信模型的效果。

claims.claim: LIME能为任何分类器的预测提供忠实且可解释的局部解释。
SP-LIME能选择一组有代表性的实例解释，帮助用户全局理解模型。
解释有助于用户评估个体预测的信任度、在模型间做出选择、改进不可信模型以及识别模型不可信的原因。
LIME在模拟和真人实验中均优于基线方法（如Parzen、贪心方法）。
LIME是模型无关的，适用于任何分类器。

limitations.limitation: 可解释表示（如词袋、超像素）可能无法捕捉某些模型行为（如色调预测）。
局部线性模型可能无法忠实近似高度非线性的局部行为。
解释的复杂度（如特征数量K）需要预先设定，可能不适用于所有用户。
SP-LIME的特征重要性度量（如文本中的√∑|Wij|）是启发式的，可能不适用于所有领域。

nodes.title: 问题定义与信任框架
nodes.label: 问题定义
nodes.summary: 定义信任的两个层面：信任个体预测和信任整个模型。指出解释预测是解决信任问题的关键。
nodes.description: 论文指出，用户需要信任个体预测以采取行动，也需要信任模型以部署。解释预测是建立信任的核心手段。

nodes.title: 可解释表示与解释模型
nodes.label: 可解释表示
nodes.summary: 定义可解释数据表示（如文本的词袋、图像的超像素）和解释模型类G（如线性模型、决策树）。
nodes.description: 解释模型g∈G作用于可解释表示的二元向量（存在/缺失）。复杂度Ω(g)衡量解释的复杂性（如线性模型中非零权重的数量）。

nodes.title: LIME目标函数
nodes.label: LIME优化目标
nodes.summary: LIME通过最小化局部加权损失L(f,g,πx)并约束解释复杂度Ω(g)来获得局部忠实解释。
nodes.description: 目标函数为ξ(x) = argmin_{g∈G} L(f,g,πx) + Ω(g)，其中L是局部加权平方损失，πx是距离度量。

nodes.title: LIME采样与近似
nodes.label: 采样过程
nodes.summary: 通过扰动输入实例生成样本，用黑盒模型预测作为标签，拟合局部解释模型。
nodes.description: 在可解释表示空间中随机采样非零元素，得到扰动样本z'，映射回原始表示z并获取f(z)。用这些样本和权重πx(z)拟合解释模型g。

nodes.title: 稀疏线性解释实现
nodes.label: 线性解释实现
nodes.summary: 对于文本和图像，使用稀疏线性模型作为解释，通过Lasso选择前K个特征。
nodes.description: 设置Ω(g)为当非零权重数量超过K时无穷大。通过Lasso（带正则化）选择K个特征，然后在这些特征上拟合加权线性模型。

nodes.title: SP-LIME：子模选择
nodes.label: SP-LIME
nodes.summary: SP-LIME通过子模优化选择一组实例，以最大化对重要特征的覆盖，同时避免解释冗余。
nodes.description: 构建解释矩阵W，定义特征重要性Ij和覆盖函数c(V,W,I)。通过贪心算法求解子模最大化问题，选择B个实例。

nodes.title: 模拟实验：忠实度评估
nodes.label: 忠实度实验
nodes.summary: 在可解释模型（稀疏逻辑回归、决策树）上，通过召回真正重要特征来评估LIME解释的忠实度。
nodes.description: 在情感分析数据集上，比较LIME、Parzen、贪心方法和随机方法。LIME在两种模型和两个数据集上均达到>90%的召回率。

nodes.title: 模拟实验：信任评估与模型选择
nodes.label: 信任与模型选择实验
nodes.summary: 模拟用户基于解释评估个体预测的信任度，以及在模型间做出选择。
nodes.description: 在情感分析数据集上，LIME在信任评估的F1分数上显著优于其他方法。在模型选择实验中，SP-LIME结合LIME表现最佳。

nodes.title: 真人实验：模型选择与特征工程
nodes.label: 真人实验
nodes.summary: 真人用户基于解释选择更优模型，并通过解释指导特征工程以改进不可信模型。
nodes.description: 在宗教分类任务上，用户基于LIME解释能更好识别泛化能力差的模型。在特征工程实验中，用户通过解释识别并删除无关特征，显著提升模型在真实数据上的准确率。

nodes.title: 真人实验：识别不可信模型
nodes.label: 识别不可信模型
nodes.summary: 通过解释帮助用户识别模型依赖错误特征（如背景雪地）进行预测的问题。
nodes.description: 在狼与哈士奇分类任务中，一个故意训练的坏模型依赖雪地背景。用户通过LIME解释能识别出这一模式，并降低对模型的信任。

deltas.before: 全局代理模型（如Parzen）试图全局近似黑盒模型，可能不忠实且计算成本高。
deltas.after: LIME专注于局部近似，通过加权采样确保局部忠实性，且模型无关。
deltas.why_it_matters: 局部忠实性对于解释单个预测至关重要，且模型无关性使其适用于任何分类器。

deltas.before: 贪心方法通过逐个扰动特征来估计重要性，可能遗漏特征交互。
deltas.after: LIME通过同时扰动多个特征并拟合线性模型，能捕捉特征重要性。
deltas.why_it_matters: 能更准确地恢复模型真正使用的特征，尤其在特征交互重要时。

deltas.before: 依赖验证集准确率评估模型，可能因数据泄露或数据集偏移而误导。
deltas.after: SP-LIME通过选择一组解释实例，揭示模型在重要特征上的行为，帮助识别泛化问题。
deltas.why_it_matters: 提供超越准确率的洞察，帮助用户识别模型不可信的原因（如依赖泄露特征）。

deltas.before: 解释方法可能产生冗余解释，用户需要查看大量实例。
deltas.after: SP-LIME通过子模优化选择非冗余、有代表性的实例，最大化特征覆盖。
deltas.why_it_matters: 在有限注意力下，为用户提供对模型行为的全面概览。

variables.description: 可解释模型（如线性模型）

formulas.intuition: LIME的核心优化目标：在保证解释简单（低Ω(g)）的前提下，找到在实例x附近能最好拟合黑盒模型f行为的解释模型g。损失L衡量局部忠实性，πx确保关注局部区域。

variables.description: 原始表示中的扰动样本

variables.name: z'
variables.description: 可解释表示中的扰动样本

variables.name: \pi_x(z)
variables.description: 样本z与实例x的距离权重

formulas.intuition: 局部加权平方损失的具体形式。通过扰动样本z'及其对应的黑盒预测f(z)来拟合解释模型g，权重πx(z)确保更靠近x的样本影响更大。
距离度量的具体形式（指数核）。σ控制局部区域的宽度，σ越小，局部性越强。论文中通过交叉验证选择σ。

variables.name: w_g
variables.description: 线性解释模型g的权重向量

variables.name: K
variables.description: 解释中允许的最大特征数

formulas.intuition: 对于稀疏线性解释，复杂度Ω(g)定义为：如果非零权重数量超过K，则复杂度为无穷大（即不允许）。这强制解释是稀疏的、可理解的。

formulas.intuition: SP-LIME的覆盖函数。衡量选择的实例集合V覆盖了多少重要特征（权重>0）。目标是最大化这个覆盖。

steps.description: 1. 获取或构建所需数据集（情感分析、20 newsgroups、宗教网页、狼与哈士奇图像）。
2. 使用scikit-learn训练黑盒模型（DT, LR, NN, SVM, RF）。
3. 实现LIME算法：定义可解释表示、采样过程、局部加权损失、稀疏线性解释（Lasso选择特征）。
4. 实现SP-LIME算法：构建解释矩阵、计算特征重要性、实现子模覆盖函数和贪心选择。
5. 运行模拟实验：评估忠实度（召回重要特征）、信任评估（F1分数）、模型选择（准确率）。
6. 进行真人实验：招募用户进行模型选择、特征工程、识别不可信模型任务。
7. 分析结果，与基线方法（Parzen、贪心）比较。

metadata.title: “Why Should I Trust You?”: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
metadata.venue: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
metadata.paper_type: Classical ML / Random Forest / Top-cited ML method paper
metadata.abstract: Despite widespread adoption, machine learning models remain mostly black boxes. Understanding the reasons behind predictions is, however, quite important in assessing trust, which is fundamental if one plans to take action based on a prediction, or when choosing whether to deploy a new model. Such understanding also provides insights into the model, which can be used to transform an untrustworthy model or prediction into a trustworthy one. In this work, we propose LIME, a novel explanation technique that explains the predictions of any classifier in an interpretable and faithful manner, by learning an interpretable model locally varound the prediction. We also propose a method to explain models by presenting representative individual predictions and their explanations in a non-redundant way, framing the task as a submodular optimization problem. We demonstrate the flexibility of these methods by explaining different models for text (e.g. random forests) and image classification (e.g. neural networks). We show the utility of explanations via novel experiments, both simulated and with human subjects, on various scenarios that require trust: deciding if one should trust a prediction, choosing between models, improving an untrustworthy classifier, and identifying why a classifier should not be trusted.

3.1 Interpretable Data Representations

Before we present the explanation system, it is impor- tant to distinguish between features and interpretable data representations. As mentioned before, interpretable expla- nations need to use a representation that is understandable to humans, regardless of the actual features used by the model. For example, a possible interpretable representation for text classiﬁcation is a binary vector indicating the pres- ence or absence of a word, even though the classiﬁer may use more complex (and incomprehensible) features such as word embeddings. Likewise for image classiﬁcation, an in- terpretable representation may be a binary vector indicating the “presence” or “absence” of a contiguous patch of similar pixels (a super-pixel), while the classiﬁer may represent the image as a tensor with three color channels per pixel. We propose to give a global understanding of the model by explaining a set of individual instances. This approach is still model agnostic, and is complementary to computing summary statistics such as held-out accuracy. Even though explanations of multiple instances can be insightful, these instances need to be selected judiciously,

SIMULATED USER EXPERIMENTS In this section, we present simulated user experiments to evaluate the utility of explanations in trust-related tasks. In particular, we address the following questions: (1) Are the explanations faithful to the model, (2) Can the explanations aid users in ascertaining trust in predictions, and (3) Are the explanations useful for evaluating the model as a whole. Code and data for replicating our experiments are available at https://github.com/marcotcr/lime-experiments.
5.1 Experiment Setup
We use two sentiment analysis datasets ( books and DVDs, 2000 instances each) where the task is to classify prod- uct reviews as positive or negative [ 4]. We train decision

We also include random forests (with 1000 trees) trained with the average word2vec embedding [19] (RF), a model that is impossible to interpret without a technique like LIME. RELATED WORK The problems with relying on validation set accuracy as the primary measure of trust have been well studied. Practi- tioners consistently overestimate their model’s accuracy [ 20], propagate feedback loops [23], or fail to notice data leaks [14]. In order to address these issues, researchers have proposed tools like Gestalt [21] and Modeltracker [1], which help users navigate individual instances. These tools are complemen- tary to LIME in terms of explaining models, since they do not address the problem of explaining individual predictions. Further, our submodular pick procedure can be incorporated
in such tools to aid users in navigating larger datasets.

Some recent work aims to anticipate failures in machine learning, speciﬁcally for vision tasks [ 3, 29]. Letting users know when the systems are likely to fail can lead to an increase in trust, by avoiding “silly mistakes” [ 8]. These solutions either require additional annotations and feature engineering that is speciﬁc to vision tasks or do not provide insight into why a decision should not be trusted. Further- more, they assume that the current evaluation metrics are reliable, which may not be the case if problems such as data leakage are present. Other recent work [ 11] focuses on ex- posing users to diﬀerent kinds of mistakes (our pick step). Interestingly, the subjects in their study did not notice the serious problems in the 20 newsgroups data even after look-
ing at many mistakes, suggesting that examining raw data

is not suﬃcient. Note that Groce et al. [11] are not alone in this regard, many researchers in the ﬁeld have unwittingly published classiﬁers that would not generalize for this task. Using LIME, we show that even non-experts are able to identify these irregularities when explanations are present. Further, LIME can complement these existing systems, and allow users to assess trust even when a prediction seems “correct” but is made for the wrong reasons. Recognizing the utility of explanations in assessing trust, many have proposed using interpretable models [ 27], espe- cially for the medical domain [ 6, 17, 26]. While such models may be appropriate for some domains, they may not apply equally well to others (e.g. a supersparse linear model [ 26] with 5 − 10 features is unsuitable for text applications). In- terpretability, in these cases, comes at the cost of ﬂexibility, accuracy, or eﬃciency. For text, EluciDebug [ 16] is a full human-in-the-loop system that shares many of our goals...
8. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we argued that trust is crucial for eﬀective

human interaction with machine learning systems, and that explaining individual predictions is important in assessing trust. We proposed LIME, a modular and extensible ap- proach to faithfully explain the predictions of any model in an interpretable manner. We also introduced SP-LIME, a method to select representative and non-redundant predic- tions, providing a global view of the model to users. Our experiments demonstrated that explanations are useful for a variety of models in trust-related tasks in the text and image domains, with both expert and non-expert users: deciding between models, assessing trust, improving untrustworthy models, and getting insights into predictions. There are a number of avenues of future work that we would like to explore.
